facts.text: The noisy friarbird is a large honeyeater with a completely bald black head apart from small tufts under the chin and along the eyebrow.
facts.quote: Its black head is completely bald apart from tufts of feathers under the chin and along the eyebrow.

facts.text: It has a rounded knob above its black bill that is visible even at a distance.
facts.quote: It can be distinguished by its rounded knob above the black bill, which is visible at distance.

facts.text: One of its calls has been likened to someone saying "four o'clock".
facts.quote: As its name suggests, it is noisy; one of its calls has been likened to "four o'clock".

facts.text: Its calls mark out feeding territories and announce food sources worth defending to other birds, not just other friarbirds.
facts.quote: The calls are used to identify an individual's feeding territory, and also announce the presence of food sources worth defending to other birds—not necessarily friarbirds alone.

facts.text: It eats nectar, insects and fruit, and raiding commercial grapes and berries can bring it into conflict with people.
facts.quote: The consumption of commercially grown fruit, such as grapes and berries, can bring noisy friarbirds into direct conflict with humans who may regard them as pests under those circumstances.

facts.text: In southern eastern Australia it is migratory, flying north to overwinter and returning south in spring.
facts.quote: In southern parts of eastern Australia the species is migratory, moving north to overwinter and returning south in the spring.

facts.text: It builds a large, deep hanging nest of bark and grass, usually well hidden one to three metres above the ground.
facts.quote: The nest is a large, deep cup with an inverted lip or rim, made of bark and grass hanging from a horizontal branch, 1–3 metres above the ground, and usually well-hidden.

facts.text: It lays two to four eggs, rarely five, splotched with darker pink-brown or purplish colours.
facts.quote: Two to four (rarely five) eggs are laid, measuring 22 by 33 millimetres (0.87 in × 1.30 in), and buff- to pale-pink splotched with darker pink-brown or purplish colours.

facts.text: It is aggressively protective of its nest and is known to swoop at intruders.
facts.quote: They are aggressively protective of their nests, and are known to swoop.
